sources.claim: Fair use (17 U.S.C. section 107) is judged case by case using four factors: purpose and character of the use, nature of the work, amount used, and effect on the market for the original. Giving credit does not by itself make a use fair; other bases for use are permission or a license, or a public-domain work.

questions.intro: Content creators build on ORIGINAL work: your own writing, photos, video, music and ideas. To use someone else's clips, songs, images or text you need a valid legal basis: permission or a license, a public-domain work, or a legal exception such as fair use, which is decided case by case. Giving credit alone is not one of these. Some platforms have tools that detect copyrighted material and may block, mute or remove content. Keep records of licenses and permissions. sections.skill: Cooking your own recipe versus copying a cookbook

questions.prompt: Your own recipe is like what?
questions.correct_answer: Original content
questions.intro: If you cook your own recipe and share it, it is yours. If you photocopy pages from a famous cookbook and post them, that is the author's work, even if you write "credit to the author." Content works the same way: original material is yours to share; for other people's material you need a valid legal basis, such as permission or a license, and credit alone is not one.
